name: Fatima Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a usual shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and have answered travel-booking calls at this contact centre for about nine years. I finished secondary school and can usually sort a missed connection, though I still ask the lead when a fare rule has changed. The pay is low for the job. I use the approved AI summary occasionally after a coworker showed me, and I always go back to the ticket before promising a refund.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Martin sells flowers at a market stall, and our children are grown and living independently. We have less than a month of expenses saved and only a few similar centres near us. I remember the family who nearly paid twice for the same journey. Martin sometimes needs a second pair of hands at the stall, but we have not counted that as my wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI Plateau is much like the summary I sometimes read, a quick note that still needs the ticket beside it. I would keep the fare check on a person’s paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think our travel calls would carry on. Still, under a month saved and Martin’s uneven market takings make me careful with each pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep handling missed-connection calls and check the AI note against the ticket before I mention a refund. In the first year of this small change, I’d put our planned new lamp aside and keep that money for the next utility bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about household money, comfortable with a small aid on the desk. The ticket, not the summary, tells me whether a passenger can travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the note miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One note said the second train was missed, but the first train had been cancelled. The fare rule changed when I read the actual journey.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you postpone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Martin (my partner) and I can use the lamp we have. We are not saving toward an investment; we are keeping cash for a bill.

say: I’d keep a **human fare check** beside AI summaries on every disputed journey.
I’d use the **actual ticket** before discussing refunds.
think: I think **travel calls** continue in the mild case.
I worry **thin savings** and uneven market takings leave us exposed.
do: Keep **missed-connection calls** and verify occasional AI notes against tickets.
Delay **new lamp purchase** and hold its cost for the next utility bill.
feel: **Anxious** about money, steady with minor software help.
S0.quote: The ticket, not the summary, tells me whether a passenger can travel.
fieldNote: Her **occasional AI use** remains tied to checking the ticket.
The **cancelled first train** changed the fare rule.
The lamp delay protects a **known bill**, without inventing spare savings.

steps.text: Keep handling missed connections and check AI notes against actual tickets
Delay buying new lamp and keep its cost for next utility bill

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will take the simple fare questions and leave people whose journey went wrong halfway through. I would ask our staff group to protect paid time for changing a ticket, not only replying to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my experience can help with complicated journeys, but the centre may pay fewer agents to do that work. With less than a month saved, even a smaller weekly wage would bite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d join coworkers sending a written request for paid ticket-correction hours and keep checking the fare rules on my assigned calls. In the first year simple questions move, I’d ask Martin whether the market can guarantee two paid morning shifts if my centre hours fall; I would not include them in our budget until he confirms actual wages and hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but able to ask for something specific. A market morning only helps if it appears as pay, not a favour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your group count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count passengers whose tickets have to be changed after an automated reply. The centre cannot use a closed-chat number to hide that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could market work pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Martin (my partner) would have to check whether the stall owner could actually pay me. He cannot promise somebody else’s wage.

say: I’d join a **paid correction-hours request** with coworkers before automated fares reduce the rota.
I’d count **changed tickets** after automated replies.
think: I think my **journey experience** may remain useful.
I fear **fewer paid agents** would cut a wage we need.
do: Join **staff request** for paid ticket corrections and keep current fare checks in 2026.
Ask about **two paid market mornings** only if centre hours fall; budget them after owner confirms wage and hours.
S1.quote: A market morning only helps if it appears as pay, not a favour.
fieldNote: The **group request** seeks paid ticket changes, not a technical demonstration.
Market hours are **uncertain** until the owner confirms pay.
She keeps **current fare checks** rather than claiming new AI learning.

steps.text: Join coworkers requesting written paid ticket-correction hours
Keep checking fare rules on assigned travel calls
Ask stall owner through Martin about two paid mornings after cuts; budget only confirmed wages/hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AGI by 2028 could answer fares and change bookings without our calls. Robots around 2031 are later, so the paid phone shift is at risk first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think most of my travel hours might go, and Martin’s stall income changes week by week. Less than a month saved would make the first missing wage a household problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d join colleagues demanding written cut dates and a paid appeal agent who can alter an unusable ticket. If my calls end in the first year after 2028, I’d ask the stall owner directly whether two paid morning shifts are available and look at posted paid local booking jobs; I would leave this job only on a signed offer with written weekly wages and hours covering our bills after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about a sudden wage gap. A flower stall can be busy and still have no wage for another worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you confirm market pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the owner for the amount and the exact days, not take a hopeful answer from Martin. I would not put the stall in our budget until that was agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the stall cannot hire?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Martin (my partner) would compare those mornings with his own stall hours. If the owner cannot pay, I will search the posted jobs rather than work for free.

say: I’d demand **written cut dates** and paid ticket appeals with coworkers.
I’d warn **2028 thinking AI** reaches booking work before robots.
think: I think **most travel hours** could disappear.
I know **under one month saved** makes the first gap serious.
do: Join colleagues’ **written notice demand** for paid ticket appeals in 2026.
Ask owner about **two paid mornings** after call loss; confirm wages/days and fit with Martin’s hours; search postings if unpaid.
Seek **posted local booking work**; leave only on signed written after-travel bill-covering weekly wages and hours.
S2.quote: A flower stall can be busy and still have no wage for another worker.
fieldNote: The **stall backup** is conditional on owner-confirmed pay and days.
She wants **appeal authority** for unusable tickets.
Her **thin cushion** makes a sudden wage loss urgent.

steps.text: Join coworkers requesting written cuts and paid ticket-correction appeals
Ask owner for two mornings after cuts; confirm wages/days fitting Martin’s hours; search postings if unpaid
Seek posted booking job; leave only on signed after-travel bill-covering weekly wages/hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives centres time to keep a person paid for awkward journeys. I would ask our staff group each year for the appeal rota and the number of changed tickets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could remain on difficult travel cases while I still earn, but full thinking AI may read those itineraries by 2031. Five years lets Martin and me see whether the stall has real paid room or only extra work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d keep handling difficult bookings and join the annual request for paid appeal hours. If the stall owner offers written paid mornings that fit my call rota, I’d take them as a second income; in the first year after 2031, if my centre hours fall, I’d apply for a posted paid local ticket desk only after checking its written weekly wages and hours cover bills after travel, leaving only on a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the end, but able to test whether either wage is real. I would rather add two paid mornings than buy a course for a job nobody has posted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would market setup be paid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the owner what the morning pays after stall setup time. A long unpaid setup could make a short shift worthless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Martin show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Martin (my partner) would show me the stall’s actual weekly sales, but I still need the owner to offer wages. Sales in a book are not my pay.

say: I’d demand **annual paid appeal rotas** with coworkers while difficult journeys still reach agents.
I’d ask for **changed-ticket counts** beside those hours.
think: I think I may keep **difficult journeys** for a while.
I doubt **stall sales** mean a wage for me without owner agreement.
do: Keep **difficult bookings** and join annual paid-appeal requests.
Take **written paid stall mornings** only if owner offers wages and shifts fit calls; compare pay with total time including setup.
Seek **posted ticket work** after call cuts only with written after-travel bill-covering weekly wages and hours; leave when signed.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to test actual wages.
S3.quote: Sales in a book are not my pay.
fieldNote: Market work requires **owner-offered wages**, including setup time.
The **staff request** ties changed tickets to paid appeal hours.
Her current wage stays until a **signed suitable offer**.

steps.text: Keep difficult booking calls while paid
Join yearly staff request for paid appeals using changed-ticket counts
Take owner-offered written paid mornings fitting calls after comparing wages against full shift including setup
Seek posted ticket job with written net bill-covering weekly wages/hours; leave on signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives the team time to keep paid human ticket changes on the rota. I would join coworkers asking for that each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I may still need my wage at 68 because Martin and I have not checked what income would continue after work. Full thinking AI could still take travel calls in 2036, with robots around 2039 later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep my paid travel calls and ask Martin to check verified later-life income against bills with me. If I still need wages after 2036 and the calls fall, I’d look at posted paid local booking roles and move only on a signed offer with written weekly wages and hours covering bills after travel; I would ask the stall owner about paid mornings only if the work is still offered then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money even with a long warning. A decade will not make the stall pay me unless someone hires me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you verify before reducing calls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check any income promised for later life before I reduce calls. I would not assume a pension amount or help from our grown children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Martin (my partner) and I would keep the grown children out of the budget. If they offered help, we could discuss a clear limit then.

say: I’d join a **yearly paid-ticket request** with coworkers while human corrections are needed.
I’d say **2036 AGI** may still take travel calls.
think: I think I may **need wages** at 68 if later-life income is too small.
I cannot assume **retirement income** before checking it.
do: Keep **paid travel calls** and join yearly coworker demands for paid ticket changes.
Verify **later-life income** against bills before reducing calls; ask about stall mornings only if still offered after 2036.
Seek **posted paid booking work** only if wages needed and calls fall; move on signed written after-travel bill-covering weekly wages/hours.

fieldNote: She treats **stall hours** as uncertain even on a decade timeline.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. It could answer fare questions and decide refunds before we have a pay plan for experienced agents. Our savings would not carry a long gap. Written staffing dates, a paid right to appeal and confirmed paid hours somewhere else would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: A passenger can get a lovely message and still have no ticket they can use. I want someone paid to check the journey and change the booking.

headlineQuote: A passenger can get a lovely message and still have no ticket they can use.
portrait: At **58**, Fatima is an experienced mid-level booking agent with average skill and secondary schooling.
She and Martin have **grown children**, low pay and under one month of expenses saved.
She uses **AI summaries occasionally** but checks the ticket before refund decisions.
She supports **paid appeal work** and considers confirmed market hours if her calls shrink.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove fare calls and refund decisions before she has another confirmed wage.
whatWouldHelp: **Written staffing dates**, paid appeals and confirmed replacement hours would help.
